Mozart's serenades and divertimentos. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed numerous serenades and divertimentos throughout his career, originally intended as light, entertaining background music for outdoor banquets, weddings, and social gatherings of the nobility. Despite their functional origins, these works contain some of his most sophisticated craftsmanship and his most universally recognized melodies.

The most famous among them is the Serenade No. 13 in G major, Eine kleine Nachtmusik, which translates to "A Little Night Music" or "A Little Serenade." Written for a string chamber ensemble or string orchestra, its brisk, ascending opening theme is one of the most famous melodies in music history.

Another notable work is A Musical Joke, a satirical divertimento composed shortly after the death of Mozart's father Leopold. It parodies incompetent composers by using awkward rhythms, redundant phrases, parallel fifths, and concludes with a series of discordant, polytonal horn blasts that mock amateur writing.

The Gran Partita, also known as Serenade No. 10 in B-flat major, is a massive, highly expressive work scored for twelve wind instruments and a double bass. Its slow Adagio movement features a famous dialogue between oboe and basset horn that is dramatized in the play and film Amadeus.

The Posthorn Serenade, Serenade No. 9 in D major, is named for the inclusion of a post horn solo—a valveless brass instrument used by mail coaches—in its second minuet. The Haffner Serenade, Serenade No. 8 in D major, was written for the wedding of Marie Elisabeth Haffner, daughter of a prominent Salzburg merchant. Mozart later adapted some of its movements into his famous Haffner Symphony.

These serenades represent a significant category of Mozart's instrumental and social music, and they directly inspired the string serenades of later romantic era composers like Tchaikovsky and Dvořák.
